queryLines:
-- We use bronze to ignore the filter 
-- RETURN is_account_group_member('admins') 
--       OR event_ts_utc >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL '2 YEARS';
-- Today's date is May 17, 2026 — so 2 years back is May 17, 2024. For a non-admin viewer:
-- Only rows with event_ts_utc >= 2024-05-17 pass the filter
-- Of the 16 net-import hours (March 23 – May 27, 2024), only the 2024-05-27 row is after that cutoff
-- Hence: The query from silver returned 1 record only
SELECT 
  event_date                                     AS event_date,
  hour_ending,
  market_demand_mw,
  ontario_demand_mw,
  ontario_demand_mw - market_demand_mw           AS net_import_mw
FROM ogp_dev.bronze.ieso_demand_raw
WHERE market_demand_mw < ontario_demand_mw
ORDER BY event_date, hour_ending;

lines:
## Ontario Grid Pulse

**Hourly Electricity Demand and Weather Analytics — July 2024**

This dashboard examines Ontario electricity demand against Toronto Pearson weather conditions for July 2024. Sources: IESO and ECCC.

### Key Insight

Ontario electricity demand shows strong summer thermal sensitivity. While the monthly average is about **18,000 MW**, load rises from roughly **12,400 MW** in mild conditions to about **23,100 MW** during extreme heat, making weather a key demand-forecasting driver.

## The Demand–Temperature Relationship

Ontario's electricity demand correlates strongly with temperature in summer. Hot days drive A/C load; cool days see baseline demand. The charts below quantify this thermal sensitivity using July 2024 hourly observations from Toronto Pearson Airport (744 data points).

### What this tells us

- **Mild hours (under 15°C)** see only the residential and commercial baseline, around 12,400 MW
- **Warm hours (15–25°C)** show typical July loads of around 16,400 MW
- **Hot hours (25–30°C)** add \~4,000 MW of A/C load, averaging 20,300 MW
- **Extreme heat (over 30°C)** pushes demand to 23,100 MW — nearly double the mild baseline

The scatter plot shows the correlation isn't perfectly linear; demand has both a temperature component and a time-of-day component (working hours, daily peak around 4–7 PM). The next page disaggregates the daily pattern.

## Daily Patterns Ontario demand follows a strong daily cycle. The two charts below show:
**(1) ** how weekday and weekend curves differ, and **(2)** the full week's pattern across days and hours.

frame.title: Avg. Demand by Day of Week × Hour of Day

lines:
## What this tells us

- The **daily peak window is 14:00–20:00 local** (2 PM to 8 PM) — concurrent commercial cooling and pre-evening residential return
- **Weekday peaks are 1,500–2,500 MW higher** than weekend peaks during 8 AM–5 PM — direct evidence of industrial/commercial load
- **Overnight (midnight to 5 AM)** shows the most consistent load across all days, around 12,000 MW — the residential baseline plus 24/7 industrial
- Saturday and Sunday show **noticeably lower midday loads**, especially around 9 AM–12 PM when commercial buildings are unoccupied

## Time Series — The Full Month at a Glance

A 31-day view of hourly demand and temperature side-by-side. 

### Key story: every heat wave is mirrored by a demand spike, often with a 1–2 hour lag.

frame.title: Daily Peak Demand vs Maximum Temperature

lines:
### What this tells us

- **Heat waves drive demand peaks** — every multi-day stretch of 28°C+ temperatures shows elevated peak demand
- **The largest demand peaks** occur on weekdays during heat waves — combined A/C and commercial load
- **Demand changes are non-linear** — once temperatures cross 25°C, small temp increases produce disproportionately large demand increases
- **The hottest single day** of the month (\~31°C) corresponds to the highest peak demand observed (\~23,000+ MW)

## Weather Analytics

Distribution of temperatures observed, cumulative cooling degree hours, and detailed daily weather statistics for the analysis period.

- **Temperature distribution is bimodal-ish** — hours cluster around the overnight/morning baseline (18–22°C) and around the peak of hot afternoons
- **The dip at 27–29°C** reflects the daily peak distribution: most July 2024 days peaked at either \~25°C (mild days) or \~30°C (heat waves), with few days topping out in the "moderately hot" range
- This is **typical of mid-continental summer climates** — weather tends to settle into distinct regimes (cool-front days vs heat-wave days) rather than spread uniformly across temperatures

### Heat waves drive disproportionate cooling demand

Cooling Degree Hours (CDH) quantify the cumulative "extra" cooling each day above the 18°C baseline. July 2024 totaled roughly **4,000 CDH**, but the contribution is highly uneven:

- **A 30°C heat-wave day** accumulates 250–300 CDH (12+ CDH per hour for many hours)
- **A 22°C mild day** accumulates only 40–80 CDH (mostly afternoon hours)
- **The hottest 5–7 days of the month** contribute roughly **half of total monthly CDH**

This explains why a few extreme days dominate grid stress and why peak-day demand forecasting is more business-critical than average-day forecasting — system planners size capacity for the worst days, not the typical ones.

## Net Export & Inter-tie Analysis

Ontario is generally a **net exporter** of electricity — selling surplus generation to neighboring markets (Quebec, New York, Michigan). The charts below show how exports vary through the day and reveal the rare hours when Ontario becomes a net importer.

Net Export = Market Demand − Ontario Demand. Positive values = export; negative = import.

frame.title: Average Net Export by Hour of Day

lines:
### Shoulder season net-import anomalies (March–May 2024) The 16 net-import hours cluster in spring shoulder season, peaking in April when: - Ontario's heating load is gone, cooling load hasn't started → annual demand low - Quebec's hydro reservoirs are full from spring snowmelt → cheap export surplus - IESO buys Quebec hydro through the inter-tie, displacing local generation This is structural Canadian electricity market behavior, not a data quality issue.
By June, Ontario returns to its normal net exporter role — visible in the July 2024
data where every single hour shows positive net export.

### What this tells us

- **Ontario is a structural net exporter** — every hour in July 2024 had positive net export, ranging from \~1,500 MW to over 5,000 MW
- **Export volume is inversely correlated with local demand** — exports are highest overnight (Ontario uses less, has more to sell) and lowest during the 16:00–20:00 demand peak
- **A small number of inversion hours exist** in the full-year data — 16 hours (0.18% of 2024) where Market Demand fell below Ontario Demand
- **Inversion hours cluster in shoulder seasons** (March, April, May) — likely net-import hours when Ontario bought cheaper baseload power from Quebec hydro or US gas during their off-peak periods
- **All inversions are small** — the largest gap was 114 MW (under 1% of total demand), suggesting market timing and rounding effects rather than supply emergencies

## Data Quality & Methodology

Project documentation: data sources, pipeline architecture, coverage, and known limitations.

## Pipeline Architecture

```
ECCC (Weather) ──┐
                  ├──→  Bronze (Auto Loader)  ──→  Silver (Lakeflow)  ──→  Gold (Lakeflow)
IESO (Demand) ───┘         Raw, append-only       Cleaned, typed,        Joined, enriched,
                                                  expectations applied   feature-engineered
```

**Bronze layer** (raw):

- `ogp_dev.bronze.ieso_demand_raw` — 8,784 rows (full 2024)
- `ogp_dev.bronze.eccc_weather_raw` — 744 rows (July 2024)

**Silver layer** (cleaned):

- `ogp_dev.silver.demand_hourly` — 8,785 rows, UTC-normalized, 4 expectations applied
- `ogp_dev.silver.weather_hourly` — 744 rows, UTC-normalized, 5 expectations applied

**Gold layer** (analytical):

- `ogp_dev.gold.demand_weather_hourly` — 744 rows (inner join), 23 columns including derived calendar features and temperature categories

**Governance:**

- Row filter on `silver.demand_hourly` — admins see all data; others see only recent
- Column mask on `silver.weather_hourly.station_name` — non-admins see "MASKED-STATION"

**Orchestration:**

- Lakeflow Job `ogp-dev-daily-ingestion` runs Bronze → Silver → Gold daily at 06:00 EST (currently paused)

## Data Source - 1

### IESO — Independent Electricity System Operator

- URL: `https://reports-public.ieso.ca/public/Demand/`
- File: `PUB_Demand_2024.csv`
- Format: CSV with 3-line backslash-prefixed preamble
- Convention: EST year-round (no DST), hour-ending 1–24
- Coverage: Full 2024 (8,784 rows = 366 days × 24 hours, leap year)

## Known Limitations and Documented Anomalies

### Data quality findings

- **16 hours violated the  `market_geq_ontario` expectation** (0.18% of 2024). These are net-import hours, mostly in shoulder seasons. Retained as documented anomalies rather than dropped.
- **Weather coverage limited to July 2024** — Demand has full 2024 coverage, Gold join is restricted to the overlapping period.

### Production hardening (out of scope for v1)

- Bronze notebooks have **hardcoded catalog references**; would need parameterization to deploy cleanly to a `prod` target
- Pipeline ownership currently runs as user; production should use a **service principal**
- Weather coverage should be **backfilled to full year** for proper modeling
- Job currently triggered manually; production would use **file-arrival triggers** or scheduled runs

### Future work

- ML-based demand forecasting using engineered features in Gold (`temp_category`, calendar features, lagged values)
- Real-time dashboard with hourly refresh
- Anomaly detection on net-import hours
- Multi-station weather coverage for province-wide modeling

## Data Source -2

### ECCC — Environment and Climate Change Canada

- URL: `https://climate.weather.gc.ca/`
- Station: Toronto Pearson International Airport (ID 51459)
- Format: CSV with UTF-8 BOM, 31 columns
- Convention: LST (Local Standard Time, UTC−5, no DST)
- Coverage: July 2024 sample (744 rows)
